title: Confinement drives valley splitting above 4K in buried silicon quantum wells
authors: Davide Degli Esposti, Emma Catherine Brann, Asser Elsayed, Davide Costa, Mark Friesen, Giordano Scappucci
abstract: Controlling the energy scales of a quantum system is essential for defining robust qubits. In silicon spin qubits, the nearly degenerate conduction-band valleys create a leakage channel from the single-spin computational basis, posing a challenge to scaling and to shuttling-based architectures. Here, we measure the relevant energy scales of single-electron spin qubits in buried silicon quantum wells co-designed for low disorder and high valley splitting. Across a linear array of four quantum dots with an average orbital energy of 2.4(2) meV, we report an average single-electron valley splitting of 0.40(6) meV and an average two-electron singlet-triplet splitting of 0.24(7) meV. In three dots, we observe a strong correlation between valley splitting and orbital energy, with an average linear coefficient of $\approx 0.22$ (meV/meV), demonstrating that electrostatic confinement can increase the valley splitting by several hundred microelectronvolts. In contrast, the remaining dot exhibits the highest valley splitting of 0.76(2) meV and low correlation, suggesting excellent characteristics for spin-qubit operation. Our findings demonstrate that strong confinement can be exploited in buried quantum wells to effectively enhance the valley splitting, thereby establishing a viable path toward the realization of shuttling and sparse-occupation-based architectures in low-disorder heterostructures.
summary: The researchers measured energy scales in single-electron spin qubits within buried silicon quantum wells to address valley degeneracy leakage. They demonstrated that by carefully engineering electrostatic confinement using gate voltages, they can significantly enhance the valley splitting ($\Delta E_V$). This finding validates a key physical mechanism for building scalable and robust solid-state quantum processors.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is mitigating leakage channels from nearly degenerate conduction-band valleys in silicon spin qubits, which hinders scaling for quantum computation.
main_result: Strong electrostatic confinement within buried silicon quantum wells can be effectively exploited to enhance the valley splitting ($\Delta E_V$), establishing a viable path for shuttling and sparse-occupation qubit architectures.
method: The study employs advanced single-electron spectroscopy techniques, including Detuning Axis Pulsed Spectroscopy (DAPS) and Pauli-Spin-Blockade (PSB) measurements, performed at cryogenic temperatures.
model_or_system: The physical system is a linear array of four quantum dots fabricated in buried silicon quantum wells ($	ext{Si}/	ext{SiGe}$ heterostructures), designed for low disorder to host single-electron spin qubits.
key_observables: Single-electron valley splitting ($\Delta E_V$), two-electron singlet-triplet splitting ($\Delta E_{ST}$), and the correlation between $\Delta E_V$ and orbital energy ($E_O$).
important_parameters: Low temperatures (e.g., $150 	ext{ mK}$); confinement strength derived from gate voltages; measured splittings in the hundred microelectronvolt range.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mapping energy scales using pulsed spectroscopy and assumes that strong confinement can be tuned via electrostatic gates to enhance valley splitting.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate device layouts, charge stability diagrams, and spectroscopic measurements showing $\Delta E_V$ dependence on gate voltages across the four quantum dots.
paper_structure: The paper details the fabrication of the heterostructure, describes the pulsed spectroscopy measurement protocols (DAPS/PSB), presents quantitative measurements of energy splittings ($\Delta E_V$, $\Delta E_{ST}$), and concludes by demonstrating that confinement engineering enhances qubit parameters.
why_interesting: This work provides crucial experimental validation for controlling fundamental energy gaps in solid-state qubits, directly impacting the feasibility roadmap for silicon quantum computing architectures.
